label: Python
description: Run a Python snippet. Declare the node's inputs and outputs inline: `ExecPython(x: Number) -> (result: String) { code: "..." }`. Every declared input is a Python variable of the same name; one that received nothing is `None`, so an optional input reads as `if problem is None`. A file input (Image, Audio, Video, Blob, File) arrives as a plain dict with `filename`, `mimeType`, `sizeBytes` and `key`, two links made for this firing, `internalUrl` to fetch the bytes from the script (`requests.get(photo['internalUrl'])`) and `externalUrl` to hand to another service, and a flag, `public`, saying whether the open internet opens `externalUrl` (when it is False, send that service the bytes instead). The links work for the file's link lifetime (15 minutes unless a LinkOptions set another) and are never written to the journal. Return a file on a file-typed output by returning that same dict. An input declared to hold a secret (`token: Secret[String]`) arrives revealed, as its value, and a value returned on an output declared as one is made a secret, so the run's record holds only its marker; what the script returns on a plain output is written down as it is. The code must return a dict keyed by output port name; a missing key emits no pulse on that port, and `return {}` emits nothing. A key set to None sends a real null on a port whose type takes it (`last: JsonDict | Null`), and emits no pulse on any other port. An exception the script raises (a request it makes failing, a `raise` of its own) fails the node with its traceback, or, with `_error` wired, comes out on `_error` instead. So does a value over 100 KB as JSON on one output (the most a wire carries): return less, or split it across outputs. Mistakes in the program always fail the run, `_error` wired or not: code that does not compile, no dict returned, a key that is not a declared output (`_error` included: raise to fail on purpose), a value of the wrong type for its port. Scripts run in a few Python processes the worker keeps and every run on it shares: a script's own variables start fresh each time, but a module it imported, anything it sets on a module, environment variables, the working directory and files it writes stay for the next script on that process, so never keep a secret or one run's data there.
